9d3b7f35-fcd1-5443-b0ea-0b06e016e0c3.title: Integrating a Product of Sine and Cosine

e-21823.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(9x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(9x-x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(9x+x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(10x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(9x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(10x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)+\frac{1}{20}\operatorname{sin}⁡(10x)]}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi ))+\frac{1}{20}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{16}(0-0)+\frac{1}{20}(0-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{20}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(12x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(12x-5x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(12x+5x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(17x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(12x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(17x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{14}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x)-\frac{1}{34}\operatorname{sin}⁡(17x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

e-21825.knowledge_point: Integrating a Product of Sine and Cosine
e-21825.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for sine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+4x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-4x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{12}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))+\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{12}(-1-1)+\frac{1}{4}(-1-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Using the product-to-sum identity, cos(11x)cos(5x) = (cos(6x)+cos(16x))/2. Integrating each term gives sin(6x)/12 + sin(16x)/32 + C, which is option a.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(11x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(11x-5x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(11x+5x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(16x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(11x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(16x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)+\frac{1}{32}\operatorname{sin}⁡(16x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

content.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(11x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(11x-5x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(11x+5x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(16x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(11x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(16x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)+\frac{1}{32}\operatorname{sin}⁡(16x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

decision.explanation: The product-to-sum identity gives cos(6x)cos(4x) = (cos(2x)+cos(10x))/2. Integrating yields sin(2x)/4+sin(10x)/20+C, matching option b.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x-4x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x+4x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(10x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(10x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\frac{1}{20}\operatorname{sin}⁡(10x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine: cos⁡(α−β)=cos⁡αcos⁡β+sin⁡αsin⁡βcos⁡(α+β)=cos⁡αcos⁡β−sin⁡αsin⁡β

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity: cos⁡(α−β)+cos⁡(α+β)=2cos⁡αcos⁡βcos⁡αcos⁡β=12(cos⁡(α−β)+cos⁡(α+β))

Thus, we have cos⁡(6x)cos⁡(4x)=12(cos⁡(6x−4x)+cos⁡(6x+4x))=12(cos⁡(2x)+cos⁡(10x)).

content.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x-4x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x+4x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(10x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(10x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\frac{1}{20}\operatorname{sin}⁡(10x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$

$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-4x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+4x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{1}{10}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(-1-0)+\frac{1}{10}(1-0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The product-to-sum identity gives cos(12x)cos(7x) = (cos(5x)+cos(19x))/2. Integrating gives sin(5x)/10+sin(19x)/38+C, matching option a.

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(12x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(12x-7x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(12x+7x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(19x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(12x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(19x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)+\frac{1}{38}\operatorname{sin}⁡(19x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

EXPLANATION

First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine: cos⁡(α−β)=cos⁡αcos⁡β+sin⁡αsin⁡βcos⁡(α+β)=cos⁡αcos⁡β−sin⁡αsin⁡β

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity: cos⁡(α−β)+cos⁡(α+β)=2cos⁡αcos⁡βcos⁡αcos⁡β=12(cos⁡(α−β)+cos⁡(α+β))

Thus, we have cos⁡(12x)cos⁡(7x)=12(cos⁡(12x−7x)+cos⁡(12x+7x))=12(cos⁡(5x)+cos⁡(19x)).

Substituting this into the integral gives ∫cos⁡(12x)cos⁡(7x)dx=∫12cos⁡(5x)+12cos⁡(19x)dx=110sin⁡(5x)+138sin⁡(19x)+C, where C is an arbitrary constant.

content.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(12x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(12x-7x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(12x+7x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(19x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(12x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(19x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)+\frac{1}{38}\operatorname{sin}⁡(19x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

decision.explanation: The product-to-sum identity gives cos(13x)cos(8x) = (cos(5x)+cos(21x))/2. Integrating gives sin(5x)/10+sin(21x)/42+C, matching option e.

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(13x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(13x-8x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(13x+8x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(21x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(13x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(21x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)+\frac{1}{42}\operatorname{sin}⁡(21x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine: cos⁡(α−β)=cos⁡αcos⁡β+sin⁡αsin⁡βcos⁡(α+β)=cos⁡αcos⁡β−sin⁡αsin⁡β

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity: cos⁡(α−β)+cos⁡(α+β)=2cos⁡αcos⁡βcos⁡αcos⁡β=12(cos⁡(α−β)+cos⁡(α+β))

Thus, we have cos⁡(13x)cos⁡(8x)=12(cos⁡(13x−8x)+cos⁡(13x+8x))=12(cos⁡(5x)+cos⁡(21x)).

Substituting this into the integral gives ∫cos⁡(13x)cos⁡(8x)dx=∫12cos⁡(5x)+12cos⁡(21x)dx=110sin⁡(5x)+142sin⁡(21x)+C, where C is an arbitrary constant.

content.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(13x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(13x-8x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(13x+8x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(21x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(13x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(21x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)+\frac{1}{42}\operatorname{sin}⁡(21x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

decision.explanation: Using sin(12x)sin(5x) = (cos(7x)-cos(17x))/2, integration gives sin(7x)/14-sin(17x)/34+C, matching option b.

after.name: Question 6
after.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(12x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(12x-5x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(12x+5x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(17x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(12x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(17x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{14}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x)-\frac{1}{34}\operatorname{sin}⁡(17x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

EXPLANATION

First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine: cos⁡(α−β)=cos⁡αcos⁡β+sin⁡αsin⁡βcos⁡(α+β)=cos⁡αcos⁡β−sin⁡αsin⁡β

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity: cos⁡(α−β)−cos⁡(α+β)=2sin⁡αsin⁡βsin⁡αsin⁡β=12(cos⁡(α−β)−cos⁡(α+β))

Thus, we have sin⁡(12x)sin⁡(5x)=12(cos⁡(12x−5x)−cos⁡(12x+5x))=12(cos⁡(7x)−cos⁡(17x)).

Substituting this into the integral gives ∫sin⁡(12x)sin⁡(5x)dx=∫12cos⁡(7x)−12cos⁡(17x)dx=114sin⁡(7x)−134sin⁡(17x)+C, where C is an arbitrary constant.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option b. The integrand is (cos(7x)-cos(17x))/2, so its antiderivative is sin(7x)/14-sin(17x)/34+C. Differentiation verifies this; option e has coefficients twice as large.

content.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(12x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(12x-5x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(12x+5x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(17x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(12x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(17x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{14}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x)-\frac{1}{34}\operatorname{sin}⁡(17x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

decision.explanation: Using sin(5x)sin(x) = (cos(4x)-cos(6x))/2, integration gives sin(4x)/8-sin(6x)/12+C, matching option e.

after.name: Question 8
after.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x-x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x+x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

content.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x-x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x+x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

after.name: Question 9
after.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(9x-2x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(9x+2x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(11x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(11x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{14}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x)-\frac{1}{22}\operatorname{sin}⁡(11x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

Thus, we have sin⁡(9x)sin⁡(2x)=12(cos⁡(9x−2x)−cos⁡(9x+2x))=12(cos⁡(7x)−cos⁡(11x)).

First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(9x-2x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(9x+2x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(11x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(11x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{14}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x)-\frac{1}{22}\operatorname{sin}⁡(11x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

$$

$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(9x+3x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(9x-3x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(12x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(12x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{24}\operatorname{cos}⁡(12x)-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{24}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{12}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{24}(1-1)-\frac{1}{12}(-1-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}

decision.explanation: Using sin(13x)cos(x) = (sin(14x)+sin(12x))/2, integration gives -cos(14x)/28-cos(12x)/24+C, matching option a.

after.name: Question 13
after.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for sine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(13x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(13x+x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(13x-x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(14x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(12x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(13x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(14x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(12x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{28}\operatorname{cos}⁡(14x)-\frac{1}{24}\operatorname{cos}⁡(12x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Product of Sine and Cosine
content.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for sine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(13x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(13x+x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(13x-x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(14x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(12x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(13x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(14x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(12x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{28}\operatorname{cos}⁡(14x)-\frac{1}{24}\operatorname{cos}⁡(12x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for sine: sin⁡(α+β)=sin⁡αcos⁡β+cos⁡αsin⁡βsin⁡(α−β)=sin⁡αcos⁡β−cos⁡αsin⁡β

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity: sin⁡(α+β)+sin⁡(α−β)=2sin⁡αcos⁡βsin⁡αcos⁡β=12(sin⁡(α+β)+sin⁡(α−β))

Thus, we have sin⁡(9x)cos⁡(x)=12(sin⁡(9x+x)+sin⁡(9x−x))=12(sin⁡(10x)+sin⁡(8x)).

Substituting this into the integral gives ∫π/2πsin⁡(9x)cos⁡(x)dx=∫π/2π12sin⁡(10x)+12sin⁡(8x)dx=[−120cos⁡(10x)−116cos⁡(8x)]π/2π=−120(cos⁡(10π)−cos⁡(5π))−116(cos⁡(8π)−cos⁡(4π))=−120(1−(−1))−116(1−1)=−110.

content.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for sine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(9x+x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(9x-x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(10x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(10x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{20}\operatorname{cos}⁡(10x)-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =-\frac{1}{20}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(10\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\pi ))-\frac{1}{16}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(8\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\pi )) \\  & =-\frac{1}{20}(1-(-1))-\frac{1}{16}(1-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$
